overview.body:
**Nakula** (*nakula*) ​— Twin ‌of Sahadeva, ‌Master of ​Horses · ​Son of ​the Aśvins ​and Mādrī ​— twin ‌of Sahadeva, ​fourth of ​the Pāṇḍu ‌princes, master ​of horses ‌— belongs ​to the ‌Sanskrit tradition, ​where it ​is catalogued ​under the ​domain "Twin, ​Son of ‌Madri". The ​name means ‌"Son of ​the Aśvins ‌and Mādrī ​— twin ‌of Sahadeva, ​fourth of ‌the Pāṇḍu ​princes, master ​of horses"[^1].

‌**Nakula** is ‌the fourth ‌Pāṇḍava: son ​of the ​Aśvin twins ‌by Pāṇḍu’s ​second queen ​Mādrī, twin ‌of Sahadeva, ​master of ​horses, swords, ‌and the lore ​of cattle. ‌The epic’s ​verdict on ​his beauty ​is unambiguous ​— among ‌the five, ‌Nakula was ​the most ‌beautiful — ​and his ​quiet competence ‌made him ‌the brother ‌wars could ‌not unsettle.[^2]

​PuniCodex restores ‌the name ​as **Nakula** ​and serves ​its temple ‌at [its ​temple](https://punicodex.com/nakula/). The ​restoration aSCII-equivalent ​form — ‌a description ​computed from ​the displayed ​form itself. ‌The plain ​ASCII form ‌*nakula* survives ​as a ‌modern convenience ​imposed by ‌the early ‌domain-name system; ​the restoration, ​not the ​fallback, is ​the form ‌the project ‌defends as ​philologically complete[^3].

the-name.body:
The ​name is ‌attested ‌in ​Devanagari as ​**नकुल**. ​Etymologically ​it means ​"Son ‌of ​the Aśvins ​and ‌Mādrī ​— twin ‌of ​Sahadeva, ‌fourth of ​the ​Pāṇḍu ​princes, master ​of ​horses"[^1].

‌The ASCII ​form ‌*nakula* ​survives only ‌because ​the ‌early domain-name ​system ‌could ​not carry ​diacritics; ‌it ‌is a ‌technological ​compromise, ​not an ‌ancient ​spelling. ​The Unicode ‌restoration ​**Nakula** ​recovers the ‌full ​diacritic detail ‌of ​the ​scholarly transliteration ​directly ​in ‌the address ‌bar. ​The ‌restoration aSCII-equivalent ​form ​— ‌a description ‌computed ‌from ‌the displayed ​form ‌itself.

​The letter-by-letter ​transformation ​runs:

- ‌**n** → ​**N** ​— ​Same, capitalized
- ‌**a** ​→ ​**a** — ​Same
- ‌**k** ​→ **k** ‌— ​Same
- ‌**u** → ​**u** ‌— ‌Same
- **l** ​→ ​**l** ​— Same
- ​**a** ‌→ ‌**a** — ​Same

pronunciation.body:
The ​reconstructed ‌pronunciation of ‌the ​name ​is ​**/nəˈkuːlə/** — ​Sanskrit ​(IAST: ‌Nakula).[^1]

​Phoneme by ​phoneme:

- ‌**Na-** ​— ‌Short a, ​light ‌n; ​the ​name is ​usually ​read ​as ‌“mongoose” or ​“of ‌the ​mongoose”.
- ‌**-ku-** — ​Long ‌ū ​as ‌in “cool”; ​the ​name ‌flows ‌without heavy ‌stress.
- ​**-la** ​— ‌Liquid l; ​the ​fourth ‌Pāṇḍava, ​master of ​horses ‌and ​swords.

‌For the ​modern ​speaker, ​the ​closest approximation ‌is: ‌“nuh-KOO-luh”

​Kindred ‌and historical ​forms ​of ‌the ‌name:

- **Twin** ‌— ‌Sahadeva ​— ‌the two ​are ​the ​Aśvin-born ‌pair
- **Parents** ​— ​the ​Aśvins ‌(the divine ​physicians), ​by ​Mādrī

‌Twin of ​Sahadeva, ‌fourth ​of ‌the Pāṇḍu ​princes ‌— ‌the ​handsomest of ​the ​five ​by ‌the epic’s ‌own ​verdict.

domains.body:
**Nakula** ​is the ‌fourth ‌Pāṇḍava: son ​of ​the Aśvin ​twins ​by ​Pāṇḍu’s second ‌queen ​Mādrī, twin ​of ‌Sahadeva, master ​of ‌horses, swords, ​and ‌the lore ​of ​cattle. The ​epic’s ​verdict on ​his ‌beauty ​is unambiguous ‌— ​among the ‌five, ​Nakula was ‌the ​most beautiful ‌— ​and his ​quiet ‌competence made ‌him ‌the brother ​wars ​could ‌not unsettle.[^1]

### ​The ​Aśvin-Born

Conceived ‌by ​Mādrī’s mantra-call ​to ‌the divine ​twin ‌physicians — ​hence ​the brothers’ ​medical ​genius.

### Master ‌of ‌Horses

​His care ‌of ​horses was ​legendary; ‌in the ‌incognito ‌year he ‌served ​as Virāṭa’s ‌horse-groom, ​a master ​among ​masters.

### The ‌Sword

​His ​blade-work the ​epic ‌ranks first ​among ​the brothers ​— ‌the quiet ​specialist ‌of the ​five.

### ‌Cattle-Lore

He ​knew ‌herds as ‌he ​knew ​horses — ​the ​brother of ‌the ‌epic’s animal-husbandry ​books.

symbols.body:
The ​iconography ‌associated ‌with ​Nakula ​concentrates ​in a ​small ​set ‌of ​recurring ​attributes, ‌each ​a ‌compressed ​statement ‌about ​the name:[^1]

- ​**The ​Aśvin-Born** ​— ​Conceived ‌by ​Mādrī’s ‌mantra-call ​to ‌the ​divine ‌twin physicians ​— ‌hence ​the ​brothers’ ‌medical ‌genius.
- ‌**Master ​of ​Horses** ‌— ​His care ​of ‌horses ​was ​legendary; ‌in ​the ‌incognito ​year ​he ​served ​as Virāṭa’s ‌horse-groom, ‌a ​master ‌among ​masters.
- ​**The ‌Sword** ‌— ‌His ‌blade-work ​the epic ‌ranks ​first ​among ​the ‌brothers ​— ​the ​quiet ‌specialist ​of ​the five.
- ​**Cattle-Lore** ‌— ​He ‌knew ​herds ‌as ​he ‌knew ‌horses ​— ​the brother ​of ​the ‌epic’s ‌animal-husbandry ​books.

mythology.body:
Nakula’s mythology ​is the epic ‌of the competent: the ‌twin born to ​the physician-gods, trained ​in every martial ​art, steady through exile, ​war, and loss. ​He has no ‌single great myth because ​his greatness was ​distributed — the ‌brother who never ​failed at anything assigned ‌to him, and ​whose death on ‌the final mountain ​was the quietest of ​the five.[^1]

### The ​Second Mantra-Birth (Ādi ​Parvan)

After Kuntī bore ​three sons by ‌mantra, Pāṇḍu asked ​Mādrī to use ‌the boon; she called ​not one god ‌but the Aśvin ​twins, and bore ‌the twins Nakula and ​Sahadeva — radiant, ‌the epic says, ​as the gods themselves. ​When Pāṇḍu died, ‌Mādrī entered his ‌funeral pyre, leaving ‌the twins to Kuntī’s ​care: the youngest ​of five mothers’ ‌sons.[^2]

### Granthika the ​Groom (Virāṭa Parvan)

In ​the thirteenth year ‌of exile, spent ​incognito, Nakula served King ​Virāṭa as Granthika ‌the horse-trainer — ​so skilled that ‌the king’s herds and ​stables prospered beyond ​record. The disguise-book ​is the epic’s ​comedy of excellence: each ‌brother, hidden, cannot ‌help being the ​best at the humble ‌job assigned.

### The ​War’s Quiet Spear ​(Bhīṣma Parvan)

In ‌the great war Nakula ‌fought at the ‌head of a ‌division, slew his ​share of the hundred ‌brothers — Duhśaha ​among them — ​and was never once ​routed. The epic’s ‌tallies of his ​duels are long ​and undramatic: the record ​of a professional ‌among heroes of ​fire.

### The Fall ​on the Mountain (Svargārohaṇika)

​On the last ‌walk, Yudhiṣṭhira explained ​each brother’s fall: Bhīma ‌for gluttony, Arjuna ​for vanity, Sahadeva ‌for pride of ​wisdom. Nakula’s sin was ‌the subtlest — ‌the pride of ​beauty: ‘he thought ​none his equal in ​form’. The verdict ​completes the epic’s ‌economy: even the quietest ‌gift, treasured as ​superiority, weighs.

vedic-references.body:
The Vedas, the oldest stratum of Sanskrit scripture, contain hymns and litanies that name or allude to Nakula. Ṛgvedic, Yajurvedic, and Atharvavedic passages establish the figure's early association with twin.

The IAST restoration Nakula marks the scholarly transliteration of those Vedic passages.[^1]

upanishads.body:
The Upaniṣads shift the focus from ritual to metaphysics, reinterpreting divine names as symbols of ultimate reality. Nakula appears or is implied in passages that map the pantheon onto the self and the cosmos.

The restored form Nakula carries the diacritic precision of Sanskrit scholarship.[^1]

puranas.body:
The Purāṇas narrate the myths, genealogies, and iconographies of Nakula in encyclopedic Sanskrit compendia. Texts such as the Viṣṇu Purāṇa, Śiva Purāṇa, and Devībhāgavata Purāṇa shape the devotional identity of the figure.

The IAST form Nakula is the scholarly anchor across these compendia.[^1]

mantras.body:
Mantras and stotras addressed to Nakula encode the name in ritual sound, often accompanied by visualizations and offerings. The syllabic structure of Sanskrit lends itself to sonic veneration.

The restored spelling Nakula preserves the precise phonetic value used in recitation and scholarly citation.[^1]
